comment.body:
Removed `ReportJson` and its test. The resolver now reads `state.json` with the application's `JsonMapper` into a `JsonNode`, from the file and from the probed live report alike, with `micronaut-json-core` as an implementation dependency of the module. I used the tree rather than a typed record so that the report format can evolve in core without failing the whole read. The probe no longer pattern-matches the first KB: it parses the served report and checks its version. Escapes and the other edge cases are now Jackson's. Without a `JsonMapper` bean the panel still renders and lists the commands, without results (24ff9d06, 8eb6d3ea).

_🤖 Addressed by [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)_

Replaced the constraint with `implementation(libs.org.json)`, so the published POM now declares org.json 20260814 at runtime scope. Added `verifyPatchedOrgJson` (run by `check`), which reads the generated POM and fails if it doesn't declare the catalog's org.json version.

_🤖 Addressed by [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)_

Fixed in 20d6e08c0f: The stub sync and async transports implement the versioned delete with `external_gte` semantics (and `deleteVersions`), with repository-level blocking and reactive versioned delete tests including the stale case.

Fixed in cf6928f1f7: With a language override the PostgreSQL vector renders the override alone (no `coalesce(<@Language column>, ...)`), so rows with their own language are analysed like the query terms; guide and `SearchQuery.Builder.language` javadoc say so and that MongoDB `$text` documents keep their indexed language; tests TextSearchCriteriaSpec (SQL) and PostgresTextSearchSpec (row with `language = 'english'` matched by `bakers` with `simple`).

comment.body:
Recommendation for the remaining part (startup failure): merge as is, and fix the leak upstream in LangChain4j rather than working around it here.

**Where the leak is.** `InfinispanEmbeddingStore(ConfigurationBuilder, InfinispanStoreConfiguration)` creates `new RemoteCacheManager(builder.build())` in a local variable, then calls `rmc.administration().schemas().createOrUpdate(schema)` and `rmc.getCache(...)`. If either call throws, the manager has already started but no reference to it escapes, so neither the generated factory nor `InfinispanEmbeddingStoreStopper` can stop it. On the success path the stopper does reach it through `remoteCache().getRemoteCacheContainer()`, and the context-close regression covers that.

**The workaround we could do, and why I don't recommend it.** The other constructor, `InfinispanEmbeddingStore(RemoteCacheManager, InfinispanStoreConfiguration)`, would let us own the manager: create it in a hand-written factory, wrap the store creation in try/catch, and stop the manager on failure. But that constructor assumes the manager already has the marshalling set up, and it never registers the schema. So we would have to:
- copy the constructor's setup into our factory: `LangchainSchemaCreator.buildSchema`, registering the proto file, the two `LangChain*Marshaller`s, `createOrUpdate(schema)` and the cache configuration;
- replace the `@Lang4jConfig`-generated factory and configuration with hand-written ones.

That copies about 25 lines of LangChain4j internals that we would then need to keep in step on every upgrade, and it moves this module off the generated pattern every other store uses. All to cover a case where the context has already failed to start: in a normal application the process exits. The leak only matters when something keeps retrying startup in the same JVM, such as tests or dev reload.

**Upstream fix.** About five lines in the LangChain4j constructor: wrap the schema registration and `getCache` in `try { ... } catch (RuntimeException e) { rmc.stop(); throw e; }`. Ideally the store would also implement `AutoCloseable`, which would let us delete `InfinispanEmbeddingStoreStopper` too. Once that is released, the leak is fixed here with just a version bump.

Happy to switch to the hand-written factory if you think the startup-failure case is worth the duplication.

### Feature description

At the moment, beans that are not injected by interface (e.g. they don't implement any interface) cannot be replaced using `@MockBean` (see https://github.com/micronaut-projects/micronaut-test/issues/535). This is a commons source of frustration as there is no warning or failure from the compiler when someone do so. See README of https://github.com/csbiggar/micronaut-mockbean-issue for full steps / an example which will recreate this issue, but in summary

In a `@MicronautTest`, mock Datastore as follows

```
    @Inject
    lateinit var datastore: Datastore

    fun mockDatastore(): Datastore {
        return mockk(relaxed = true)
    }
```

Run the test (via your IDE or using `./gradlew test` )

### Actual Behaviour

```
	at io.micronaut.context.DefaultBeanContext.doCreateBean(DefaultBeanContext.java:1925)

	at io.micronaut.context.ProviderUtils$MemoizingProvider.get(ProviderUtils.java:60)
	at io.micronaut.context.DefaultBeanContext.getScopedBeanForDefinition(DefaultBeanContext.java:2372)
	....
```
Full stack trace here:

issue.body:
### Expected Behavior

In MicronautJunit5Extension, the `beforeAll` method puts the `ApplicationContext` into the JUnit `ExtensionContext` (https://github.com/micronaut-projects/micronaut-test/blob/v3.9.2/test-junit5/src/main/java/io/micronaut/test/extensions/junit5/MicronautJunit5Extension.java#L85)

When `rebuildContext = true`, then the `ApplicationContext` is re-assigned to a new pointer (https://github.com/micronaut-projects/micronaut-test/blob/v3.9.2/test-core/src/main/java/io/micronaut/test/extensions/AbstractMicronautExtension.java#L361-L366) but the old pointer is still retained by `ExtensionContext`

I have my own extension for helping with cross cutting concerns in Micronaut tests and I use the `ExtensionContext` to get the `ApplicationContext`.  I think this is causing issues for me when I run with `rebuildContext = true`

See attached reproducing application

The expected behavior is that the `ApplicationContext` in the extension and the `ApplicationContext` injected in the test should be the same for each test method

### Actual Behaviour

When running the attached application, you can see the `ApplicationContext` injected into the test differs each time

But the `ApplicationContext` known by the extension is not updated:

```
09:46:13.385 [main] INFO  i.m.context.env.DefaultEnvironment - Established active environments: [test]
09:46:13.964 [main] ERROR com.example.MyJUnit5Extension - ApplicationContext = io.micronaut.context.DefaultApplicationContext@4e9658b5
09:46:13.973 [main] ERROR com.example.DemoTest - ApplicationContext = io.micronaut.context.DefaultApplicationContext@4e9658b5

09:46:14.195 [main] ERROR com.example.DemoTest - ApplicationContext = io.micronaut.context.DefaultApplicationContext@251ebf23

...
```

### Steps To Reproduce

Run `mvn clean test` using the attached example application

[demo.zip](https://github.com/micronaut-projects/micronaut-test/files/11355728/demo.zip)

I was able to hack my way around this but I do not know how best to do it cleanly.  The `ApplicationContext` is recreated by `AbstractMicronautExtension` which does not know about the JUnit `ExtensionContext` and there is no easy way to call back to `MicronautJunit5Extension`

EDIT: I guess maybe the naive way is maybe the best way; simply call `store.put(ApplicationContext.class, applicationContext);` inside `MicronautJunit5Extension.beforeEach` every time

### Environment Information

JDK 17
Micronaut 3.9.0
Linux

https://github.com/micronaut-projects/micronaut-test/files/11355728/demo.zip

comment.body: Consolidated into #2886.

Done (24ff9d06). The probe now has three outcomes: this project, unknown, or none. A probed live report with a missing or blank `project` counts as unknown: the panel says continuous testing may be running, and neither links to that report nor shows its results. A live process's report that names no URL is linked to the default address only on a confirmed match. Lenient matching stays only for `state.json` read from this project's own directory. Tests cover each case, and the panel text and the guide say so.

_🤖 Addressed by [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)_

[P2] Preserve existing duplicate-name pairs when adding another cookie

Indexing all received pairs by name silently removes unrelated cookies. For example, mutating `Cookie: sid=app; sid=root; theme=dark` with `cookie(Cookie.of("trace", "1"))` now emits `sid=root; theme=dark; trace=1`, dropping `sid=app` even though the caller did not change `sid`.

Duplicate names in a received Cookie header are valid when cookies have different Path or Domain attributes ([RFC 6265 §4.2.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6265#section-4.2.2)). A proxy filter adding an unrelated cookie should forward those pairs intact; dropping one can change the session seen by the upstream application.

Please preserve the ordered existing pairs whose name differs from `name`, and apply replacement only to the cookie being explicitly set. I reproduced this through both `NettyHttpRequest.mutate()` and the `MutableServerRequest` filter overlay: both regression tests pass on base `b89e265` and fail on this head, with the output above.

comment.body: The guarantee stated here ("never inspected", "does not show its connection settings", and the motivating case of an account that must not run ad hoc queries) only holds for the datasource panel. `HibernateControlPanel`/`HibernateRuntimeService` build `HibernateDataSourceInfo` (JDBC URL, driver, catalog, schema, pool sizes) from the session factory bound to the same datasource and expose the HQL console for it, and nothing in the Hibernate module consults `DataSourceControlPanel.enabledProperty(name)`. Could you either have the Hibernate panel honour the same property for the session factory's datasource name, or qualify the sentence here to say that the setting applies to the datasource panel only and that the Hibernate panel has its own `micronaut.control-panel.panels.hibernate.enabled` switch?

This is the point from my previous review that the rewrite did not pick up: `micronaut.control-panel.panels.datasource.datasources.<name>.enabled` is still resolved with `Environment.getProperty`, so it does not appear in the generated configuration reference (`controlPanels.adoc` includes `ControlPanelConfiguration` from `configurationProperties/`), gets no IDE metadata, and the guide section in `datasource.adoc` has to be hand-written. Could you back it with a small `@EachProperty(DataSourceControlPanel.DATASOURCES_PREFIX)` configuration class (one bean per datasource name with an `enabled` flag, default `true`) and look it up with `BeanLocator.findBean(..., Qualifiers.byName(beanName))`, then include the generated properties file in the docs instead of the YAML snippet?

`index.hbs` renders every panel's body on the dashboard and on the Dashboard category page, so with this constructor each of those page loads now performs `dumpAllThreads(true, true)` (a safepoint plus monitor/synchronizer walk the Javadoc flags as potentially expensive) and then formats every frame of every thread into strings, only for `body.hbs` to print `total` and the per-state counts. The first version of this PR took a depth-0 `getThreadInfo(getAllThreadIds(), 0)` snapshot for the card and reserved the full dump for the detail view; the rewrite dropped that. Could the card path go back to the cheap snapshot (still through the `ThreadInfoMapper`, since a depth-0 `ThreadInfo` is still a `ThreadInfo`), for instance by keeping `ThreadInfo` in the row and formatting the stack/lock lines lazily, or by taking the full dump only when the detail view is being rendered?

This test runs in the `nativeTest` job too (the E2E suite only opts individual methods out with `@DisabledInNativeImage`, and `AbstractE2ETest` has explicit native-image bootstrapping), but in a native image `ThreadMXBean.dumpAllThreads(true, true)` returns an empty array (`SubstrateThreadMXBean` returns an empty array), which the guide text you added also says. The page then renders "No threads were reported..." with no `details.cp-thread-stack`, so `containsText("RUNNABLE")` and the `firstStack.locator("summary").click()` will fail once the queued native job runs. Either annotate the test with `@DisabledInNativeImage` like `testDatasource`/`testKafka`, or branch on `NativeImageUtils.inImageCode()` and assert the empty-state text there, which would also pin down the behaviour the docs describe.

Thanks for switching this to a real `r2dbc.datasources` configuration with an actual `ConnectionPool`; that covers the part that bit us last time. The other half of my earlier comment still stands though: nothing renders `views/r2dbc/body.hbs` / `detail.hbs`, so a typo in a model field name (`factory.pool.maxAllocated`, `usagePercent`, `maxPendingLimited`, ...) would only show up in a browser, and unlike every other module (`control-panel-kafka`, `-hibernate`, `-datasource`, `-cache`, `-object-storage`) this one is not wired into `doc-examples/example-java`, so neither `ControlPanelRenderingTest` nor the Playwright suite exercises it. Adding the module plus an `r2dbc:pool:h2:mem:` datasource to the example app (behind an optional environment if you prefer) and asserting on the rendered detail page would close that gap and give the guide screenshot a permanent home.

This covers the panel bean and the inspector well, but nothing in the PR compiles or renders `views/opensearch/body.hbs` or `detail.hbs`: the module is not added to `doc-examples/example-java` (so there is no `ControlPanelRenderingTest`/E2E coverage) and the module tests never go through `ControlPanelRenderer`. issue.body:
I was reading over an article by Quarkus which discusses async consumers and when to commit offsets:
https://quarkus.io/blog/kafka-commit-strategies/

It seems that it is using `SmallRye` kafka connector behind the scenes, and recommends the `throtttled` strategy to achieve highest throughput with reactive consumers, while still guaranteeing that offsets committed periodically aren't accidentally done for records which haven't completed processing.

Currently, the only way to get this working in Micronaut is to use reactive types, but then to manually acknowledge each consumer record, which reduces the throughput and adds load to the broker, OR to use `@Blocking` on the consumer.

### Feature description

Problem: 
A `KafkaConsumer` instance can be safely shared between threads when all access is `mutually exclusive`. Improper access results in a `ConcurrentModificationException` being raised - as per the [documentation](https://kafka.apache.org/32/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer/KafkaConsumer.html#multithreaded).

Feature Request:
To ensure that Micronaut's use of `KafkaConsumer`s is mutually exclusive, achieved by performing Kafka operations within a `synchronized` block. 

Implementation:
- Synchronise access to `KafkaConsumer` instances within the `KafkaConsumerProcessor` when performing Kafka operations.
- Update documentation in `ConsumerRegistry#getConsumer`.

labels.description: A minor improvement to an existing feature

issue.body:
We're building a set of Kafka consumers on Micronaut and keep running into a gap that I think would be worth closing upstream.

When you want to know how a consumer is actually doing — how many records it processed, how long processing took, and whether each one succeeded or ended up dead-lettered — there's no framework-level hook for it today. What Micronaut currently gives you is:

- the Kafka client binder metrics (`kafka.consumer.fetch.manager.*` via `micronaut.metrics.binders.kafka.*`), which are transport-level and don't say anything about your application's processing outcome, and
- distributed tracing through `micronaut-tracing` / OpenTelemetry.

So the processing outcome itself you end up instrumenting by hand. The natural approach is an AOP interceptor around the listener method — but that fires once per invocation, and since Micronaut retries by re-invoking the method, a record that fails a couple of times before succeeding gets counted several times. You can't get a clean per-message outcome, or a clean retry count, from user code.

That's really the crux of it: only the consumer / error-strategy layer knows where one attempt ends and where a record is finally *done* (either processed or dead-lettered). So it's the only place that can record the outcome exactly once per message and count retries correctly. Anything sitting on the listener method is a layer too high.

Spring Kafka already does this, which is where the idea comes from — its listener container manages `spring.kafka.listener` timers (`result=success|failure`, `exception`) and, with `observationEnabled`, creates an Observation per record with a customizable `KafkaListenerObservationConvention` / `DefaultKafkaListenerObservationConvention`. Micronaut has the building blocks too: the general Observation API support landed in micronaut-micrometer (#585), and there's already a `micronaut-micrometer-observation-http` module doing the equivalent for HTTP.

Rough shape of what we have in mind:

- an `Observation` created around each record's processing by the consumer pipeline, so it wraps the terminal outcome and is retry-aware, gated behind a config flag;
- a context + convention pair (something like `KafkaListenerObservationContext` / `KafkaListenerObservationConvention`) with a sensible default that adds group id / topic tags, the same way the HTTP module does it;
- a receiver context, so teams that want trace propagation get it for free, while metric-only users just get the timer.

We'd be happy to put up a PR if the direction is agreeable. Mainly wanted to sanity-check it with you first, and ask where you'd prefer it to live — directly in micronaut-kafka (where the listener and retry lifecycle are), or as a `micronaut-micrometer-observation-kafka` module mirroring the HTTP one.

Versions we're on: micronaut-kafka 5.10.x (Micronaut 4.x), micronaut-micrometer 5.13.x, Micrometer 1.16.x.

issue.title: Add a per-stream option to leave the consumer group during graceful Kafka Streams shutdown
issue.body:
### Feature description

**Feature request**
Please add an opt-in setting for each named Kafka Streams configuration that explicitly leaves its consumer group when that stream is gracefully closed. The proposed setting is kafka.streams.<stream-name>.leave-group-on-close.

**Motivation**
When a Kafka Streams instance shuts down, the application may need its group membership to end promptly so that remaining instances can take over its partitions. An explicit leave-group operation makes that intent clear during a planned shutdown and can reduce the time before work is reassigned.
This matters especially for applications that define multiple named streams. Those streams may serve different workloads and have different shutdown requirements, so a single application-wide setting would not provide enough control.

**Desired behavior**

- The setting is configurable independently for each named stream.
- When enabled, a gracefully closed stream explicitly leaves its consumer group, using that stream’s configured close timeout.
- When disabled or omitted, the stream retains its current shutdown behavior. The default should be false to preserve compatibility.
- The setting affects shutdown only. It should not close a stream during creation or be passed to Kafka Streams as a client configuration property.
- The behaviour should apply whether shutdown is initiated through Micronaut’s graceful-shutdown lifecycle or normal application-context destruction.

**Acceptance criteria**
Tests should demonstrate that two named streams with different settings use their respective shutdown behaviors and timeouts, that an omitted setting preserves existing behavior, and that creating a stream does not close it.

issue.title: Keep H2's shutdown hook out of the first development generation
issue.body:
Development mode warned "retired generation(s) [1] are still reachable" on most reloads of the Java and Kotlin petclinics. The warning was right: generation 1 stayed reachable from H2's shutdown hook.

H2 creates `OnExitDatabaseCloser.INSTANCE`, a thread it registers with `Runtime.addShutdownHook`, the first time a database is opened with `DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=TRUE` (the default for file databases; in-memory URLs such as `jdbc:h2:mem:devDb;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=TRUE` set it explicitly). The thread takes the context class loader of the thread that first opens a database, which under the launcher is generation 1's application thread:

```
ApplicationShutdownHooks.hooks → org.h2.engine.OnExitDatabaseCloser → contextClassLoader → GenerationClassLoader (generation 1)
```

The thread is never started, so `GenerationThreads.release`, which re-points live threads, never sees it. This adds the class to `GenerationMemory.PARENT_TIER_STATICS`, so that the launcher initializes it with the parent tier's loader, as it already does for UCP.

`H2ShutdownHookGenerationMemoryTest` runs a probe in its own JVM: generation 1 opens such a database, and the test checks that the hook is registered, that its context class loader is not a generation's, and that generation 1 is collected. It fails without the change.

Tracked in #13654 (gap C2).

issue.title: Hold Hikari's thread-local connection lists weakly in development mode
issue.body:
Every datasource edit in development mode left the closed `HikariPool` alive: after a full GC the Kotlin petclinic held 8 pools, 7 of them closed.

Hikari's `ConcurrentBag.requite` caches returned connections in a per-bag thread-local list. The list's value reaches its own key (`PoolEntry → HikariPool → connectionBag → threadLocalList`), so the entry is never cleared, and `close()` only clears the closing thread's list. The Netty event loops are retained across restarts, so each one keeps every pool it ever borrowed from:

```
NonBlockingFastThreadLocalThread → threadLocals → FastList → PoolEntry → HikariPool
```

Hikari holds those entries weakly when `com.zaxxer.hikari.useWeakReferences=true`, or when it is not loaded by the system class loader; in development mode the parent tier is the system class loader. The development runtime now sets the property when it is unset and Hikari is on the parent tier. No production code changes.

`HikariThreadLocalsGenerationMemoryTest` borrows and returns a connection on a long-lived thread, closes the pool from another, and checks that the pool is collected. It fails without the change.

With this and #14409, a minimal H2 + Hikari application went through 15 reloads, 5 of them datasource edits, with no warnings and one class loader and one pool left after GC.

issue.title: Keep the event publisher of each event type in the bean context

labels.name: repo-44764586
labels.description: A minor improvement to an existing feature

issue.body:
Part of the bean resolution stack (#14368).

`BeanContext.publishEvent` and `publishEventAsync` looked up `ApplicationEventPublisher<EventType>` on every call. That definition is not a singleton, so every published event ran a full bean creation (resolution context, path segment, creation tracking, registration) only to reach the publisher the factory already memoizes per event type, with its listeners. The context now keeps the publisher of each event type it published, bounded like the candidate caches and dropped with them, so a replaced publisher definition or a stopped context is picked up. Only the built-in publisher (`ApplicationEventPublisherFactory`, which already keeps one publisher per event type) is kept: a publisher of another definition keeps its own scope, a prototype one still being created for every event. The cache write is guarded by the definitions epoch, as the candidate caches are, so an answer that raced a registration is not kept.

Adds a `publishEvent` scenario (one listener) to `BeanResolutionBenchmark`: 251 → 5.8 ns, 904 → 0 B/op. Adds `PublishEventPublisherCacheSpec` (sync and async events reach the listeners of their type; after a stop and start a new listener is reached; a primary prototype publisher of another definition is created for every event).

Behaviour note: a `BeanCreatedEventListener` of `ApplicationEventPublisher` no longer sees a creation of the built-in publisher per published event, only the first one per event type.

issue.title: Resolve runtime proxy targets through a copy of the resolution context
issue.body:
Fixes micronaut-projects/pyronaut#411.

A runtime proxy whose target is a `@Prototype` bean (in Pyronaut PetClinic, `ClinicService` with `@Transactional` methods) resolves the target through the resolution context kept by `DefaultRuntimeProxyDefinition`, on every call and from several threads at once. `around()` kept the live context of the proxy's creation, so concurrent resolutions shared and corrupted its path, giving spurious `CircularDependencyException` and `BeanInstantiationException` errors under load.

`around()` now also keeps a `copyForLazyProxyTarget` copy, as compiled lazy proxies do, and `targetBean()` resolves through it, so `DefaultBeanContext` creates each target in a fresh copy. The one exception is a target resolved on the creating thread while the proxy is still being created, as a creator that caches its target does. That one still uses the live context, so the target stays a dependent of the proxy and is destroyed with it.

Tests (`ConcurrentProxyTargetTest`):
- resolves the prototype target from 16 threads, 200 times each. It failed before with the corrupted path from the issue.
- checks that a target cached while the proxy is created is destroyed with the proxy. It fails if the copy is used for that resolution too.

The AOP tests in `inject-java` and the Python proxy specs (`-Ppython-ci`) pass, as do checkstyle, spotless and `japiCmp` on `aop`.

issue.title: Graph support 23/24: Batch relationship writes, make graph writes atomic and add @Relationship(cascade)
issue.body:
Part of #4218. Stacked on the AGE tenants PR; review the diff against `stack/graph/24-age-tenants`.

Three write-path findings from the review of the graph feature against its plan.

**Relationship links are batched.** Nodes of a `saveAll` were already written with one `UNWIND`, but every relationship link was its own `MATCH … MERGE`. `GraphQueryBuilder.buildLinksQuery` now renders one statement per relationship type over `$rows` (`position`, `from`, `to`, `properties`):

```cypher
UNWIND $rows AS row MATCH (a:Movie), (b:Person) WHERE a.title = row.from AND b.id = row.to
MERGE (a)<-[r:ACTED_IN]-(b) SET r += row.properties RETURN row.position AS position, id(r) AS id
```

The runtime first saves the target nodes of each relationship property in a batch (new ones through the node `UNWIND`, existing ones through a batched update), then merges the links grouped by relationship property. AGE 1.5 cannot `MERGE` a relationship per `UNWIND` row, so its batched statement keeps the `OPTIONAL MATCH … CREATE … UNION … SET` shape the single link used. Saving 3 movies with 2 roles each went from 13 statements to 7 (`1 + 2N` instead of `1 + 4NM`), asserted by counting the TRACE log in `Neo4jOperationsSpec`. Dynamic relationships are still written one at a time.

**Writes are atomic.** `persist`, `persistAll`, `update`, `updateAll`, `delete` and `deleteAll(entities)` run inside `transactionOperations.executeWrite` (Neo4j and AGE JDBC) or `withTransactionMono/Flux` (Neo4j and AGE R2DBC), joining an outer `@Transactional` when one is active, so a cascading save that fails half-way leaves nothing behind. The TCK checks a save whose relationship fails after a cascaded node was written, and the schemaless and reactive specs check an invalid dynamic label. Oracle graph delegates its writes to Micronaut Data JDBC and R2DBC and is unchanged.

**`@Relationship(cascade = …)`** with `Relation.Cascade` semantics: `ALL` (the default, today's behaviour), `PERSIST` (new nodes created, existing ones linked without an update), `UPDATE` (existing nodes updated, a new one fails), `NONE` (the relationship only; the node must have an identifier and exist, otherwise a `DataAccessException` and nothing written). The member is kept apart from `Relation.cascade` so Oracle's JDBC path is not affected.

```java
@Relationship(value = "KNOWS", cascade = Relation.Cascade.NONE)
private List<Person> knows = new ArrayList<>();
```

Documented in the mapping page ("Saving relationships" and a new "Cascading to related nodes" section) with `snippet::` includes from the Java, Kotlin, Groovy and Python examples. The Python example's `testShortestPath`/`testPathOptions` were failing on the base branch (a Python instance converts to a distinct Java twin per reference, so the same person was merged twice); they now reuse the instance returned by `save`.

Not in this PR: `CypherQueryBuilder.java` is past the checkstyle file-length limit (tolerated by the build); splitting its renderers into their own files is a follow-up noted in the plan.
